title: Parallel Hadamard Test
abstract: The Hadamard test is a fundamental building block widely used in many quantum computing algorithms. It estimates the real or imaginary part of $\langle ψ\vert U \vert ψ\rangle$, where $\vert ψ\rangle$ is a quantum state and $U$ is a unitary operator. In many algorithms, however, many such quantities must be estimated, leading to a large number of distinct circuit types, long computational times, and high financial costs. In this work, we propose the parallel Hadamard test, which combines multiple Hadamard tests into a single circuit type. We demonstrate how the parallel Hadamard test applies to three structural classes of workloads: arbitrary sets of unitary operators, prefix-product arrays, and Gram-matrix elements. For each class, we compare the cost of the parallel Hadamard test with that of the conventional one. Our unified approach significantly reduces the number of distinct circuit types, and can lower both computational time and financial costs in regimes where fixed per-circuit overheads dominate the total cost. In Gram-matrix workloads, it can also reduce the total number of shots when typical off-diagonal overlaps are small.
summary: The paper introduces the Parallel Hadamard Test (PHT) to overcome the exponential growth of distinct circuits needed when estimating many quantum expectation values. By combining multiple standard Hadamard Tests into one circuit, PHT significantly reduces computational and financial overheads across various quantum workloads, including VQA gradient estimation and kernel calculations.
main_problem: The conventional estimation of multiple quantum expectation values, such as those required for gradient calculation or kernel evaluation, leads to a proliferation of distinct quantum circuits.
main_result: The proposed Parallel Hadamard Test (PHT) unifies these estimations into a single circuit type, significantly reducing overheads in terms of circuit count, time, and cost across various workload structures.
method: PHT combines multiple independent Hadamard Tests (HTs)—used to estimate $	ext{Re}[\langle\psi|U|\psiangle]$ or $	ext{Im}[\langle\psi|U|\psiangle]$—into one optimized quantum circuit structure.
model_or_system: The work is general, applying to three structural classes of workloads: arbitrary sets of unitary operators (e.g., VQA gradients), prefix-product arrays (e.g., QCELS), and Gram-matrix elements (quantum kernel methods).
key_observables: Expectation values $	ext{Re}[\langle\psi|U|\psiangle]$ and $	ext{Im}[\langle\psi|U|\psiangle]$, energy expectation values $\langle H angle$, and gradients $ rac{\partial\langle H angle}{\partial	heta_j}$.
important_parameters: The required precision ($\epsilon$) dictates the number of shots; fixed per-circuit overheads become critical when many estimations are needed.
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes that hardware supports mid-circuit measurement and reset (MCMR) to implement PHT efficiently, and that typical off-diagonal overlaps are small for shot reduction in Gram-matrix settings.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the standard HT circuit, VQE circuits, gradient estimation circuits, and the core PHT structure showing how multiple estimations are combined into one gate preparation $V_{+W}(M)$.
paper_structure: The paper introduces the fundamental problem of estimating $\langle\psi|U|\psiangle$ via HT. It then proposes PHT as a unified solution, demonstrating its applicability and cost savings across three distinct structural classes: arbitrary sets, prefix-product arrays, and Gram matrices.
why_interesting: This work directly addresses resource optimization in quantum algorithms by providing a hardware-aware compilation technique that minimizes circuit overheads, which is crucial for running complex variational algorithms on NISQ devices.
